profiles.description: Adam Lee Heimerman, an independent candidate for Tennessee’s 2nd Congressional District, was arrested on July 30, 2026 after investigators accused him of shooting four automated license-plate-reader systems in Blount County and Maryville. He was booked into the Blount County Correctional Facility on bonds totaling $40,000. The county’s current-inmate roster no longer listed him on September 28.

Investigators reported finding a sticker reading “DeFlock” with a link to an anti-surveillance camera map. Williams faces felony arson, criminal-damage, and interference-with-government-property counts and a reckless-conduct count. profiles.name: James F. Hitselberger
profiles.description: James F. Hitselberger is a former Navy contract linguist who worked with the Fifth Fleet in Bahrain. Military investigators accused him in 2012 of taking classified documents from a secure work area; one document was later found in the Hoover Institution archives at Stanford University. Prosecutors initially charged him under the Espionage Act with unauthorized retention of national-defense information. He spent 54 days without bond in the District of Columbia jail before a judge released him on December 19, 2012 to strict home confinement and electronic monitoring. In April 2014 the government replaced the Espionage Act charge with a misdemeanor count of unauthorized removal and retention of classified documents. Hitselberger pleaded guilty and was sentenced on July 17, 2014 to time served and a $250 fine.
profiles.finding: Hoover collection and FAS case files identify linguist; physician obituary born1927 is unrelated.
profiles.rights: No image accepted; public accessibility not treated as public-domain status

profiles.name: James Brice
profiles.description: James Brice was prosecuted in Blount County, Tennessee, for stealing an enslaved person. In May 1814 Tennessee’s highest court rejected his appeal in Brice v. State, holding that a colonial-era North Carolina law making the offense capital remained in force in Tennessee. Brice was hanged on July 20, 1814. The reported decision documents the prosecution and the legal rule but does not identify the enslaved person or establish that Brice acted from an abolitionist motive.
profiles.finding: Governor James Brice died1801, excluded from1814 execution profile; no subject portrait found.
profiles.rights: No image accepted; public accessibility not treated as public-domain status

profiles.name: Joseph Weir
profiles.description: Joseph Weir was convicted in North Carolina in a scheme to carry away several enslaved people. The state’s supreme court record says an accomplice testified that preparations were made at Weir’s house and that Weir supplied a model for forged bills of sale, later returning the papers with a false seller’s signature. The court allowed the accomplice testimony and forged documents to support the verdict. Weir was hanged on June 20, 1828. The record describes a planned theft supported by false sale papers rather than documenting abolitionist activity.
profiles.finding: Modern university scholar and genealogy person died1809 excluded from1828 execution profile.
profiles.rights: No image accepted; public accessibility not treated as public-domain status

profiles.name: Littleton Prince
profiles.description: Littleton Prince was prosecuted in Pike County, Alabama, for “negro stealing” after being accused of carrying away two enslaved people. Alabama archival records show that he escaped jail and was later arrested in Savannah, Georgia, for return to Alabama. Prince maintained that he was innocent, and one of the enslaved people reportedly supported his account, but the conviction stood. He was hanged in 1833. No surviving evidence found in this review ties him to an abolitionist organization, so his motive remains unresolved.
profiles.finding: No portrait located; Baron Hatherton image unrelated.
profiles.rights: No image accepted; public accessibility not treated as public-domain status

The surviving compiled record located in this review does not identify the person or people they were accused of helping, describe Evans’s individual conduct, or establish his motive.

profiles.name: Alvin Flowers
profiles.description: Alvin Flowers was among a group of white men hanged in Gadsden County, Florida, in 1846. The Espy chronology classifies Flowers, John Black, and Thomas Smith under “Aid Runaway Slave” and dates their executions to October 2. Other later execution compilations describe Flowers and the group through a mail-robbery and murder prosecution and disagree about the date. Because the surviving summaries conflict and do not separate each man’s conduct, this profile preserves the Espy classification without presenting it as a settled account of Flowers’s motive.
profiles.finding: No identity-linked portrait found for1846 Gadsden case.

profiles.name: Redding Evans
profiles.description: Redding Evans was a white farmhand, about thirty-two years old, prosecuted in Jefferson County, Florida, for “slave stealing.” Later Florida execution records identify the enslaved woman as Rose and place Evans’s hanging at Monticello on December 2, 1850. The Espy chronology more broadly classifies the case as aiding a runaway slave. The official summary is sparse, and this profile does not rely on later unsourced retellings for the details of Evans and Rose’s relationship or their attempted flight.
profiles.finding: Social retellings do not authenticate portrait; Frederick Evans image unrelated.

profiles.name: Willis Hester
profiles.description: Willis Hester was a white North Carolinian, reported to be about forty-one years old, executed at Pittsboro on May 5, 1855. The Espy and North Carolina execution records classify his offense as aiding a runaway slave. A contemporary Fayetteville Observer notice says the alleged offense occurred in Orange County and that the trial was moved to Chatham County. The brief notice supplies no account of the person Hester was accused of helping and no reliable evidence of his motive.

profiles.name: Milton Chaney
profiles.description: Milton Chaney was convicted in Lancaster District, South Carolina, of carrying away an enslaved man named Toney. The appellate record says Chaney took Toney to Virginia under the name Martin, used the alias Jerry M. Tobert, and exchanged him for an enslaved woman and $200 while presenting a purported bill of sale. The court rejected Chaney’s challenge to the evidence and upheld the conviction despite acknowledging its “terrible consequences.” He was hanged on July 11, 1856. The record describes trafficking for value, not abolitionist assistance.
profiles.finding: Modern obituary namesake and Milton/Chaney keyword matches excluded.
profiles.rights: No image accepted; public accessibility not treated as public-domain status

profiles.name: Moses Gossett
profiles.description: Moses Gossett was convicted in Union District, South Carolina, under the 1754 statute against stealing an enslaved person and aiding an enslaved person to leave an owner’s service. The court record identifies the man as Ned, claimed by James Shannon, and says Ned left in September 1854. Gossett’s appeal failed, and the Espy chronology records his hanging on July 11, 1856. The available record establishes assistance in Ned’s departure but does not establish Gossett’s broader political beliefs.
profiles.finding: Family genealogy mentions execution, but no authenticated portrait located.
profiles.rights: No image accepted; public accessibility not treated as public-domain status
